Wireheading and the Conditions of a Common

                 World

       Attention, Reward, and the Limits of Universal Self-Promotion


                                Flyxion

                              Independent Researcher

                            October 2026




                                Abstract

  Wireheading, in its original sense, is the direct activation of a reward mechanism in place

   of the activities through which that mechanism ordinarily operates. This essay argues that

  the concept names a structural hazard that extends well beyond pleasurable stimulation.

  The hazard arises when a signal of success becomes independently optimizable while

  the conditions that gave the signal its signiﬁcance are left to deteriorate. Applied to

  contemporary institutions, the claim requires care, because pleasure, entertainment,

  publicity and digital communication are not intrinsically pathological. The relevant

  question is when the production of rewarding signals begins to displace the activities and

  relationships those signals were meant to serve. The essay develops a small formal model

  of the allocation of eﬀort between substantive work and signal production, examines

  the thought experiment of a society in which everyone follows the advice to become

  a broadcaster, and draws attention to the maintenance labour on which every visible

  activity depends.  It considers institutional cases and then hypernormalization, the

  process by which a drifted measure is stabilized through the universal reproduction of its

  form, which obstructs correction either by concealing private doubt or, where dysfunction

   is openly acknowledged, by leaving knowledge without a means of organized change. It

  states a material limit on the labour that can be allocated outside provisioning, and two

  requirements of viability, one concerning the availability of dissent, illustrated by the

  premise of Minority Report, and one concerning the diversity of modes of work. It then

  distinguishes the documentation of an activity, which can add to its value, from the

  organization of an activity around its publishability, which can distort it, and illustrates

  the distinction with two cases: recordings of ordinary domestic labour as demonstration

  data for robotic manipulation, and a class of lightweight, paper-based, string-actuated

  robots designed to make their own construction and upkeep intelligible. After addressing

  the objection from paternalism, the essay proposes a universalizability test for attention

  strategies and a set of design questions concerned with preserving the possibility of


                                    1

correction. Its conclusion is that the deepest danger of wireheading is the progressive

       loss of the capacity to notice and repair the diﬀerence between feeling rewarded and

       living well.


1. From Reward to Its Artiﬁcial Satisfaction


The experiments of Olds and Milner in the early 1950s established that rats would press

a lever in order to deliver electrical stimulation to certain regions of their own brains [22].

The result was striking for what it suggested about the architecture of motivation. Reward,

in an ordinary organism, is a regulatory signal that is activated through engagement with a

world: through eating, exploring, mating, solving, caring. The electrode short-circuits the

engagement and delivers the signal directly. The signal remains, but the conditions that

made it informative have been removed. In the vocabulary that later became standard, the

organism has been wireheaded.

   The term has since travelled. In the literature on reinforcement learning and artiﬁcial

agents, it describes a system that modiﬁes its own reward channel, or the sensory inputs

from which reward is computed, rather than improving its performance at the task the

reward was designed to elicit [24, 9]. Related phenomena go under the names of reward

hacking and speciﬁcation gaming [1, 32]. In moral philosophy, Nozick’s experience machine

poses a cognate question about whether the felt quality of experience is the only thing that

matters, and his negative verdict, that most people would decline to plug in, is usually taken

to show that we care about actually doing and being certain things and not merely about

the experience of doing and being them [21]. Neuroscientiﬁc work distinguishing the wanting

of a reward from the liking of it adds a further complication: the machinery that drives

pursuit is dissociable from the machinery that registers pleasure, so that a system can be

strongly motivated toward a signal that no longer delivers what it once did [3].

   This essay is concerned with a broader and more deliberately analogical use of the concept.

A person watching videos is not an organism with an electrode in its septal region, and

an institution pursuing publicity is not an agent modifying its own reward function in the

technical sense. The analogy concerns the separation of reinforcement from the conditions

that would make reinforcement informative. Where such a separation opens, the system

acquires the ability to register success without acquiring a corresponding ability to sustain

whatever success was supposed to mean. The governing question of the essay is accordingly

the following. What happens when a system becomes increasingly eﬀective at producing and

detecting signals of success, while its eﬀectiveness at maintaining the activities, relationships

and material conditions to which those signals referred does not keep pace, or declines?

   Two cautions frame the discussion.  First, the analogy is not oﬀered as a moralistic

indictment of pleasure, leisure, entertainment or publicity. Each of these can be, and very


                                       2

often is, part of a worthwhile life and a well-functioning society. The argument concerns

a structural relationship between signal and activity, and it can be stated without any

assumption that screens are bad or that everyone ought to be perpetually productive.

Second, the analogy has limits. Where the essay describes institutions as wireheaded, it

means that their reinforcement structures exhibit a particular gap, and it does not mean

that their members are deluded, cynical or complicit. Much of the interest of the topic lies in

the fact that the gap can open and widen among participants who are sincere and diligent.


2. The Signal and the Activity


Recognition can indicate worthwhile achievement. Revenue can help sustain useful production.

Audience engagement can accompany meaningful communication. In each case the signal is

correlated with an underlying good, and the correlation is the reason the signal is worth

pursuing and worth using as a basis for allocating resources. The diﬃculty is that each

signal also admits strategies that improve its measurement without improving its object.

This regularity has been stated in several forms: Goodhart’s observation that a statistical

regularity tends to collapse once it is used for control, Campbell’s law that the more a

quantitative indicator is used for social decision making the more it distorts the processes

it was intended to monitor, and Strathern’s compact formulation that when a measure

becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure [13, 5, 35]. Muller’s book-length treatment

documents the pattern across education, medicine, policing and business [20].

    It is important to see why the problem is stronger than dishonesty. A common response

to metric distortion is to suppose that it results from gaming by unscrupulous actors, and

that it could be eliminated by better monitoring and sterner penalties. The more troubling

cases are those in which participants sincerely follow the incentives available to them. A

researcher who writes proposals in the style that funding panels reward, a teacher who

prepares students for the form of an examination, and a creator who learns which thumbnails

are clicked are all responding rationally to the signal as it is presented. The distortion

emerges at the level of the system when the incentives systematically reward the production

of appearances, responses or measurements more reliably than the work they are meant to

recognize.

  A minimal model makes the structure explicit. Consider an agent with a unit budget of

eﬀort, to be divided between substantive work w and signal production p, so that w + p = 1

with w, p ≥0. The substantive value produced is V = a w for some a > 0. The observable

signal is S = b w + c p, where b > 0 measures how well substantive work is registered by the

signalling channel and c > 0 measures how eﬀectively direct signal production is registered.
The agent is rewarded by the signal, and bears a convex allocation cost κ2(w2 + p2) with

of activity. The agent therefore chooses w to maximize

   The proposition is elementary, but the interpretation is not. The parameter c is not ﬁxed

by nature, and it is worth considering how it might vary with the competitive environment.

One particular escalation scenario arises where the signal is positional, so that rewards

depend on rank and not on level. If the eﬀectiveness of promotional eﬀort rises with the

number of rivals who also promote, for instance because each competitor must match the

promotion of the others merely to hold its place, then one may write c = c0 + γ(n −1) for

n competitors and some γ > 0. This form is an additional assumption and is not derived

from competition as such. Crowding can equally reduce the eﬀectiveness of promotion, since

audiences saturate and distinguishing marks lose their force, and in some environments c

would fall with n. Under the escalation assumption, the proposition implies that substantive

eﬀort declines as the ﬁeld becomes more crowded, even though no individual has become less

honest or less capable. Hirsch’s analysis of positional goods and Frank and Cook’s account

of winner-take-all markets describe dynamics of this kind in other vocabularies [16, 12].

Rosen’s economics of superstars supplies a related explanation of why small diﬀerences in

measured standing can translate into large diﬀerences in reward, which can raise the returns

to marginal signal production in some settings [25].

   The model also clariﬁes what is and is not being claimed.  It does not claim that

c > b in every domain, nor that signal production is worthless.  In domains where the

signalling channel registers substantive work well, so that b is large relative to c, the system

rewards substance and behaves well. The claim is that the relationship between b and c is a

contingent and revisable property of the institutional environment, that it can drift, and

that participants following local incentives will not in general be positioned to notice the

drift.



                                       4

3. Attention as Both a Resource and an Obligation


A prominent piece of contemporary advice holds that everyone should cultivate an audience,

build a personal brand and maintain a continuous public presence. The advice has an evident

basis. Neglected work does sometimes remain neglected for want of any means of being

found, and publicity can correct that. Public communication also helps to coordinate people

who would otherwise not know of one another’s existence or interests. These beneﬁts are

real, and an account of attention that ignored them would be tendentious.

    Nevertheless, attention has features that complicate its treatment as an ordinary resource

to be acquired. Herbert Simon observed in 1971 that a wealth of information creates a

poverty of attention, and that the design problem of an information-rich world is the eﬃcient

allocation of a scarce capacity among the sources that might consume it [31]. Attention

is ﬁnite per person, and it cannot be accumulated or stored.  It is also unusually rival

in a particular sense: attention directed to one source is attention withdrawn from every

other. A strategy that succeeds for one participant by capturing more attention therefore

succeeds, to the extent that the total is ﬁxed, by reducing what is available to others. Wu’s

history of the commercial capture of attention describes how successive media industries have

exploited exactly this structure [37], and Debord’s older analysis of the spectacle describes

the condition in which lived relations are replaced by their representation [7].

   This suggests a distinction between two kinds of communicative eﬀort. Some communi-

cation helps people coordinate: it conveys what a person can contribute, what a community

needs, how a technique is performed. Other eﬀort chieﬂy changes who gets noticed, and

has little eﬀect on what there is to notice. The ﬁrst kind has positive-sum possibilities,

since a successfully coordinated pair of parties are both better oﬀ. The second kind has

the character of a contest whose aggregate return, to the extent that attention is ﬁxed, is

bounded by the total available, while its aggregate cost is the sum of everyone’s expenditure.

Most actual communication mixes the two, and the essay does not claim that they can be

cleanly separated. The claim is that the proportion matters, and that a social environment

can raise the share of eﬀort devoted to the second kind without anyone intending it.

  A related observation concerns the relation between contribution and recognition. Curtis

contrasts the committed, largely anonymous participation he attributes to the civil rights

movement with a contemporary expectation that a commitment be made publicly visible,

since visibility is now a main source of validation [4]. His historical comparison is sweeping

and would need qualiﬁcation, since the movement had prominent ﬁgures as well as anonymous

participants. The conceptual point is nevertheless pertinent: the wish to contribute can

become entangled with the requirement to be recognized as contributing, so that the second

begins to shape what is done in the name of the ﬁrst.




                                       5

It follows that an individual’s successful publicity strategy cannot automatically be

generalized into a prescription for everyone. The fact that a given person has beneﬁted

from being visible is evidence that visibility can be beneﬁcial for that person under those

circumstances. It is not evidence that universal visibility would be beneﬁcial, or even possible.

The next section makes this precise.


4. The Universal Broadcaster


Imagine a society in which everyone follows the advice to become a broadcaster. It would

be a mistake to assume that catastrophe follows simply because people make videos. There

is nothing intrinsically ruinous about recording and sharing, and a society in which a large

fraction of the population communicated publicly might be richer in some respects than one

in which few did. The thought experiment is useful for a narrower reason: it exposes the

practical dependencies of broadcasting and the incompleteness of broadcasting as a universal

solution to livelihood.

   Broadcasting requires food, electricity, networks, buildings, equipment, maintenance and

care. It also requires audiences whose attention is not already exhausted. Let a population

of N persons each possess a time budget T. Suppose a fraction σ of total time must be

devoted to sustaining labour, meaning the production of food, the operation and repair of

infrastructure, and the care of the young, the ill and the old, and suppose a fraction ϕ of the

population broadcasts, each broadcaster devoting a fraction τ of their time to production.

The time available for viewing is then at most (1 −σ −ϕτ)NT, and the mean viewing time

received per broadcaster is
                                          (1 −σ −ϕτ) T

                                       6

The proposition concerns means, and it establishes attention dilution under the stipulated

time budget and no more. It does not show that universal participation in broadcasting

is impossible, nor that audience-based livelihoods are unattainable. A conclusion about

income would require further assumptions about how attention is converted into revenue

and about the income each broadcaster needs in order to live, and the model makes neither.

Attention is also in practice distributed very unequally across broadcasters. In heavy-tailed

environments a small number of participants receive a large share of the attention, so that the

median experience lies below the mean [25, 12], and a mean ﬁgure may therefore overstate

what a typical participant receives. The model’s purpose is the narrower structural point

that any livelihood derived from audience attention depends on audiences whose time is not

wholly committed to broadcasting, and on a population of workers, not themselves full-time

broadcasters, who sustain the conditions of both. A strategy can depend on others not

adopting it to the same degree.

  A related distinction applies to a familiar promise, namely that anyone can escape

ordinary employment by becoming a coach, an inﬂuencer, or a seller of advice about escaping

ordinary employment. The word “anyone” is ambiguous. An opportunity can be open to

any individual without being simultaneously available to everyone, just as any individual

may seek a seat in a theatre although not everyone can occupy the front row. The strongest

target of the present argument is therefore advice that presents audience-based income as a

general solution while leaving unexplained its dependence on diﬀerentiated labour and on

audiences supplied by others. Advice of this kind often has a recursive structure in which

the product sold is the strategy of selling the product. Where the revenue of the advisers

derives largely from those seeking to become advisers, the arrangement requires a continuing

inﬂow of new entrants and cannot be extended to the whole population without changing

its character. This is not to say that any particular adviser is insincere. It is to say that the

form of the oﬀer, taken as a general route to freedom, depends on a distribution of labour

and attention that its own universal adoption would alter.


5. The Hidden Work of Sustaining Experience


The preceding section turns attention from the visible content of a culture to the conditions

that make its production and consumption possible. A video must be recorded on a

device that was manufactured, transmitted over a network that is maintained, stored in

a facility that is powered, and watched by a person who has eaten, slept, and been cared

for. The activities that supply these conditions include infrastructure repair, sanitation,

food production, caregiving, teaching, and ecological maintenance. A distinctive feature of

such activities is that their beneﬁts are often less conspicuous than their interruption. A




                                       7

functioning water system attracts no attention until it fails.

   This asymmetry of visibility has been recognized in several traditions. Mierle Laderman

Ukeles’s 1969 manifesto of maintenance art distinguished a development system, associated

with individual creation, novelty and change, from a maintenance system, which keeps the

results clean, preserved and sustained, and it pressed the question of who attends to the

everyday labour that makes creative work possible [36]. Susan Leigh Star’s work on the

ethnography of infrastructure observed that infrastructure is by its nature invisible until

it breaks, and that this invisibility shapes how the labour involved is valued [34]. More

recent historical scholarship on maintenance and repair has argued that innovation receives

disproportionate attention relative to the upkeep on which most actual technological life

depends [27]. James Scott’s account of legibility makes a related point from the side of

administration: what is easily measured and displayed tends to be favoured over what is

locally embedded and diﬃcult to summarize [29].

  A distinction drawn in an interview with the scholar Andrew Russell sharpens the

asymmetry. Russell separates innovation as an activity, meaning invention and creation,

from talk about innovation, and his criticism concerns the attention that the language

attracts, since time given to it competes with time for maintenance [28]. The point ﬁts

the structure of this essay.  Innovation can register worthwhile change, but it can also

become a designation that institutions pursue independently of whether their changes

improve anything, while eﬀective maintenance attracts little recognition precisely because

it prevents conspicuous events. The criticism is not a blanket preference for preserving

existing technologies, and it does not oppose technological ambition. It also qualiﬁes any

simple valorization of upkeep. Preserving essential capacities, such as sanitation, scientiﬁc

instruments or shared knowledge, can enable substantial change, whereas maintaining an

institution’s appearance of competence, or an existing distribution of power, can obstruct it.

The relevant questions are what is being maintained, for whom, and with what capacity for

revision.

   The argument does not divide society into virtuous manual workers and frivolous cultural

workers. Art, research, entertainment and conversation can themselves sustain a worthwhile

common life, and some of the most important maintenance in a society is cultural and

intellectual: the preservation of languages, the transmission of skills, the upkeep of shared

standards of evidence. A society that left all of this unmaintained would be impoverished

in ways that no amount of material provision would repair. The distinction that matters

is therefore not between kinds of occupation. It is between activities that contribute to a

common life and activities that increasingly consume the supporting conditions of that life

merely in order to reproduce engagement. A painter whose work enriches a community is

on the right side of this distinction, and so is a repairer of pipes. A publicity apparatus



                                       8

whose output is chieﬂy more publicity, and which draws labour and attention away from the

maintenance of its own supports, is on the other side.

   Graeber’s discussion of occupations whose holders themselves doubt their usefulness is

relevant here as an example of how the relationship between reward and contribution can

come apart at the level of individual work [15]. The present essay is more cautious than

Graeber’s in one respect. Self-assessments of usefulness are an unreliable guide, and the

diﬃculty to be diagnosed is structural and not psychological. The question is whether the

reward structure of a ﬁeld tracks the contribution of the ﬁeld, and this can be examined

without relying on the opinions of those who work in it.


6. Documentation and Display


The wireheading argument is easily misapplied to recording as such, and a clear distinction

is needed. The concern raised by a society in which people constantly broadcast their

most publishable moments as photographs and videos is not that recording is bad. It is

that a particular selection process operates on what is recorded and shared. Repetition,

preparation, failed attempts and maintenance tend to disappear from public view, although

they constitute much of what makes any accomplishment possible. People then encounter a

public world composed disproportionately of exceptional moments, and some begin arranging

their own lives in order to supply such moments. The argument becomes more exact when it

concerns this feedback loop between display and the organization of activity, and less exact

when it concerns screen time or recording in general.

   The distinction can be stated as a question about the direction of dependence. Either

the feedback from recording improves the capacity to act, or action is increasingly organized

around obtaining the feedback. In the ﬁrst case documentation is subordinate to the activity:

it serves as a diagnostic, as a means of instruction, as a way of inviting correction. In the

second case the activity is subordinate to its documentation, and the form of the activity is

progressively shaped by what will display well.


6.1 Recorded labour as demonstration

A concrete illustration is provided by ordinary domestic and municipal labour. A recording

of someone collecting litter along a roadside, or washing a stack of dishes, is not an optimized

display of exceptional moments.  It captures repetition, partial failures, regrasping, the

handling of awkward objects and the sequencing of tasks. Such material can be useful in

several distinct ways. It can communicate practical technique to a human learner. It can

reveal labour that is otherwise overlooked, and thereby alter how that labour is regarded.

And it can provide examples for the study of robotic manipulation, a ﬁeld in which tasks of



                                       9

this sort remain diﬃcult. The literature on learning from demonstration treats recorded

human performance as a primary source of training signal precisely because the tasks are

hard to specify analytically [2].

   The usefulness of such recordings depends on what they capture and on how someone can

use them, and the claim made here is a modest one. Raw video is not training data in any

straightforward sense, and the translation from observed human movement to robot control

involves substantial diﬃculties of embodiment and correspondence. The relevant claim is

limited. Broadcasting is not inherently a withdrawal from useful work, and a recording

that documents mundane labour in an unoptimized way sits near the opposite end of the

spectrum from the curated highlight. Its value is largely independent of how many people

view it, and does not depend on the performer having organized the work around the camera.


6.2 Lightweight robotics and intelligible construction

A second illustration concerns the design of machines. Consider a class of lightweight robots

in which the body is constructed principally from folded or laminated paper, internal strings

transmit pulling forces to produce motion, and pneumatic components supply or regulate

actuation. For convenience these may be called pneumatic endo-marionettes. The general

family to which such designs belong includes tendon-driven mechanisms, origami-based

fabrication and soft robotics [10, 26]. The precise arrangement of strings, bladders and valves

would matter a great deal in any real design, and the present discussion does not depend on

it. What is of interest is the connection between this research direction and the observation

of ordinary tasks. Observing how a person washes a dish or lifts a bag invites the question

of what movements, compliance and contact with the environment a mechanism would need

in order to accomplish something useful, and a lightweight body with distributed internal

tension is a natural candidate for exploring that question cheaply.

   Here the distinction between documentation and display acquires a design interpretation.

Filming a prototype can help diagnose its failures, teach someone how to build it, or invite

a useful correction. The same prototype could also be optimized for an impressive clip while

remaining unreliable outside the demonstration, tuned for the one successful take and brittle

everywhere else. The ﬁrst relationship between camera and machine builds capacity. The

second builds the appearance of capacity. A research programme can be assessed in part by

asking which of these relationships its working practices tend to produce.

   The concept of a didactic robot sharpens the point. A machine might be designed so

that its own construction and maintenance are made understandable through its behaviour.

Suppose such a robot prepared itself by applying sheets of paper to its body one at a time,

so that the manner in which its structure is assembled and repaired is displayed in the course

of ordinary operation and not concealed beneath a ﬁnished exterior. The preparation would


                                       10

then be part of what is worth attending to, and not a hidden precondition. Imagine further

that a child is present while the robot, balanced on one leg, struggles to pull on a pair of

trousers and comments humorously on its predicament. The child can see the relationship

between balance, movement and the diﬃculty of dressing. The humour arises directly from

what the robot is doing, and does not require a separate stream of entertainment laid over

the activity. Limitations become occasions for shared attention and learning.

   This case reverses the publishable-moment problem. Under the logic of display, prepa-

ration, repair and failure are edited out, because they do not present well. In the didactic

design they are placed at the centre, because they are where the instructive content lies.

The robot teaches through the care it takes with ordinary tasks, including the care required

to keep itself working. The lesson generalizes. Entertainment, humour and visibility are

compatible with capacity-building when they arise from the intelligible performance of an

activity. The concern is with systematic displacement, in which the production of display

comes to replace the activity and erodes the capacities that support it. It is not that every

entertainment must itself develop capacities, a requirement the discussion of leisure below

rightly rejects.


7. Institutional Wireheading


The analysis extends well beyond social media. Several institutional cases share the analytical

structure of a widening gap between institutional reinforcement and institutional purpose.

Each would require detailed evidence in a full empirical treatment, and the following

descriptions are oﬀered as schematic illustrations of a pattern whose presence in particular

institutions must be established case by case.

  A university can become highly eﬀective at producing rankings, publicity and competitive

grant proposals while reducing the time available for teaching and inquiry. Strathern’s account

of audit culture in British higher education describes how the demands of accountability,

once internalized, reorganize the activity they were intended to oversee [35]. A business can

improve customer engagement metrics while making its service harder to leave, so that the

measured attachment of customers reﬂects the cost of departure and not the value of the

service. Hirschman’s analysis of exit, voice and loyalty is the classical statement of why the

ability to leave matters as a mechanism by which organizations learn of their own decline

[17], and an organization that suppresses exit forfeits the correction it would otherwise

receive. A public agency can satisfy reporting requirements without resolving the diﬃculties

those reports describe, so that the production of compliant documentation becomes the

eﬀective task.

   The shared structure admits a general description. Let P denote the purpose of an




                                       11

institution and M the measurement regime through which its performance is registered

and rewarded. Initially, M is a reasonable proxy for P. Participants optimize against M,

since that is what the institution rewards. Because M is a coarser object than P, there are

directions in which M can be improved at little cost to P or even at the expense of P. As

optimization proceeds, the relationship between M and P changes: the proxy relationship,

which held under the earlier distribution of behaviour, ceases to hold under the new one.

The institution continues to register improvement, and the registration appears to conﬁrm

that the institution is succeeding. Nothing in the reinforcement signal itself indicates that

the correlation has failed.

    It is worth emphasizing that this process requires neither coordinated deception nor

universally cynical participants. Each participant responds to the signals they face, and the

system as a whole drifts. The point has an uncomfortable implication: moral exhortation

directed at individual participants will have limited eﬀect, because the relevant error is

located in the structure of the reinforcement. This is also why the diagnosis has a positive

counterpart. If the gap is structural, it can be addressed by structural means, and these are

discussed in a later section.


8. Hypernormalization and the Closure of Correction


The gap between signal and purpose described in the preceding section becomes more diﬃcult

to repair when it is stabilized by a further process, for which the term hypernormalization

is available. The term derives from Alexei Yurchak’s anthropological study of the last

Soviet generation, where it names a speciﬁc development in late socialist public life [38].

Yurchak observed that after the death of Stalin the authoritative discourse of the state, in

its slogans, meetings, reports and rituals, became increasingly standardized and increasingly

reproduced in a ﬁxed form. Because the form was now ﬁxed, participants could, and did,

reproduce it exactly without any need to treat its literal content as a claim to be believed

or disbelieved. Yurchak describes this as a shift from the constative to the performative

dimension of ritualized speech: attending a meeting, voting in the approved manner or

repeating an approved phrase became acts that were valuable as acts of participation, and

their propositional meaning receded. The result was neither mass belief nor mass cynicism.

It was a condition in which the form of public life was reproduced with great ﬁdelity while

the relationship between that form and anyone’s actual assessment of the world became

largely irrelevant to the reproduction.

   Yurchak is careful to resist two simpliﬁcations that popular uses of the term have

encouraged. The ﬁrst is the binary of sincere believers and secret dissidents, a picture on

which people either endorsed the system or privately opposed it. His material shows that




                                       12

many participants found real meaning, friendship and creative life within and alongside

the reproduced forms, and that the performative shift opened spaces of activity that the

constative reading of the discourse would have prohibited. The second simpliﬁcation is the

assumption that the system’s stability was straightforwardly the result of fear. A good deal

of the stability came from the fact that the reproduced forms were the only publicly legible

ones, so that every participant had reason to expect every other participant to continue

reproducing them. The term was later extended to Western societies in Adam Curtis’s 2016

documentary HyperNormalisation, which uses it to describe a condition in which widespread

awareness that institutions are failing coexists with the absence of any credible alternative,

so that a simpliﬁed picture of the world is maintained because no other framework seems

available [6]. That extension is looser than Yurchak’s, and is Curtis’s own interpretation. It

should be treated as a suggestive use of the term and not as a ﬁnding about contemporary

societies, and it should not be read as a direct account of Yurchak’s book. In a podcast

interview about the ﬁlm, Curtis glosses Yurchak’s observation as the condition in which

everyone knows that things are not right, the leaders know that everyone knows, and nothing

is done because no other picture of the world is available. He adds that he is not claiming

that contemporary societies resemble the Soviet Union, only that they share a sense of

unreality and of leaders who lack control [4]. This is again his paraphrase and not Yurchak’s

own formulation. The present essay adopts only the structural core of Yurchak’s account,

and applies it with attention to the diﬀerences between the cases.

   The structural core can be connected directly to the model of the preceding sections.

Suppose that a measurement regime M has drifted away from its purpose P, and suppose

that many participants have private knowledge of this, whether in the form of a settled

judgment or of an inarticulate unease. Whether that knowledge becomes public depends on

the cost of expressing it relative to the cost of continuing to reproduce the form. Where

expression is costly, for instance because recognition, employment or standing depend on

visible compliance with M, each participant has reason to reproduce the form regardless of

their private assessment. Kuran’s analysis of preference falsiﬁcation describes the resulting

equilibrium: public preferences diverge from private ones, and because everyone observes

only public behaviour, each participant underestimates how many others share their doubts

[19]. The eﬀect is a form of pluralistic ignorance sustained by the very behaviour that

conceals it.

Remark 1. Let gi denote participant i’s private assessment of the gap between M and

P, and let Bi denote i’s publicly observable behaviour with respect to M. Suppose each

participant faces a cost di of public deviation and a beneﬁt ei from expressing gi, and

reproduces the standard form whenever di > ei. If di > ei holds for every participant, then

Bi takes the same value for all i whatever the values of gi, so that observed behaviour



                                       13

carries no information, through that channel, about the distribution of private assessments.

Other evidence, including gradual changes in outcomes, may of course remain available.

A system whose members are all in this regime exhibits maximal observable agreement

together with possibly large hidden divergence. If the inequality fails for some participants,

their public dissent may lower the cost of deviation for others. That is a plausible additional

mechanism, of the threshold kind familiar from models of collective behaviour [14], and it is

not established by the remark itself.

   The remark helps to explain two features that Yurchak and later commentators have

emphasized. The ﬁrst is that apparent stability is poor evidence of health. A regime in which

every observable indicator is favourable may be one in which the indicators have ceased to be

informative, because they are produced by a process that no longer depends on the state of

the thing indicated. The second is the possibility of abrupt change. Yurchak’s title records

the experience of the late Soviet period, in which the order seemed permanent until it ended,

and many observers on all sides were surprised by the manner of the end. A system that

has lost its internal channels for registering divergence may conceal accumulating divergence

until a disruption makes it publicly visible.

  Two obstructions to correction are distinct. The ﬁrst is concealed disagreement, the

condition modelled in the remark, in which public compliance hides the distribution of

private judgments. The second is the condition emphasized in Curtis’s account, in which

dysfunction is already widely acknowledged, and is known to be acknowledged, but the

acknowledgement does not issue in action because no credible alternative or capacity for

collective action is available. In that condition exposure loses its disruptive force, since

each further revelation conﬁrms what people already expect and does not change what

they think possible. Protected dissent addresses the ﬁrst obstruction and does little for the

second, which also requires institutions, coordination and suﬃciently developed proposals

through which people can do something with what they know. In the interview he points

to the large London march against the Iraq war in 2003, whose participants were sincere

and numerous but who, in his telling, then went home, and he contrasts this with sustained

commitment of the kind he attributes to the American civil rights movement. He further

suggests that Occupy and the Arab Spring stalled because they confused process with

content, that is, because they mistook their procedures of assembly and participation for an

answer to the question of what should replace the arrangements they opposed [4]. These

are his interpretations of particular episodes and are not established here, but they supply

a useful test for any activity: whether it merely expresses dissatisfaction, or develops the

means to change the conditions that produce it.

   The notion therefore describes a second-order form of the wireheading structure. In the

ﬁrst-order case, a signal of success is optimized in place of the activity it indicated. In the



                                       14

hypernormalized case, the signal that is being optimized is the appearance of normality

itself, the continued smooth reproduction of expected forms. Participants are rewarded for

not disturbing it, and the reward is real, since the stability of the form is a precondition of

their own standing. In the concealed-disagreement case, correction is then doubly obstructed.

The ﬁrst-order gap between M and P  is concealed by the reproduction of M, and the

second-order evidence that the gap exists, namely the private doubts of participants, is

concealed by the reproduction of the form of agreement. In the acknowledged-dysfunction

case the evidence is not concealed, and the second obstruction is of a diﬀerent kind: available

knowledge is not translated into organized change.

   Contemporary communication environments exhibit a version of this structure at the

level of ordinary social presentation. A feed composed of publishable moments establishes a

standard of normal life that few participants actually inhabit, and because each participant

contributes to the standard while privately knowing the gap between it and their own

experience, each is positioned to believe that the others live up to it. The mechanism

is the same as in Kuran’s analysis, applied to the presentation of lives and not to the

endorsement of policies. A diﬀerent mechanism is emphasized in Curtis’s interview, where he

argues that systems which return to users more of what they are already known to like are

conservative, since they hold the informational situation of each group stable and conceal

from each what the others know [4]. This is an interpretive claim about recommender

systems and not an established result, but it indicates a further route by which a signal of

engagement can stabilize the arrangement that produces it. The comparison should not be

pressed too far. Contemporary media environments lack the central authority of the Soviet

case, the cost of deviation is typically social and not coercive, and the forms reproduced

are decentralized products of many competing sources and not of a single discourse. The

comparison nevertheless indicates what to look for: a regime in which every visible indicator

is favourable and in which the capacity of the system to register the gap between its indicators

and its purposes has quietly disappeared.

   The point also bears on the positive proposals to be developed below.  If hypernor-

malization consists in the conversion of private knowledge of a gap into universal public

reproduction of a form, then a corrective must lower the cost of making private knowledge

public, or must supply channels through which it can inform decisions without requiring

any individual to bear the cost of open deviation. This is a diﬀerent requirement from the

introduction of better metrics, since a new metric will itself be reproduced in the same

manner if the conditions of reproduction are unchanged.





                                       15

9. Material Limits and Corrective Requirements


A further question concerns what a society can carry. If wireheading in the extended sense

is a condition in which reward has separated from the sustaining of what reward referred to,

one may ask how much of a society’s activity can be of that kind. Three considerations bear

on the question, and they have diﬀerent evidential standing. One is a material limit that

follows arithmetically from a stated provisioning model. The other two are requirements of

viability, conditions that a self-correcting society must meet, for which the analysis supplies

no quantitative thresholds. The discussion concerns functions and allocations of labour and

not classes of persons, since the same individual may occupy diﬀerent functions at diﬀerent

times.

   The material limit follows from the dependence of every visible activity on sustaining

labour, discussed earlier. Let N be the population and L ≤N the labour supply, measured

in units of full-time labour over a period. Let Ls be the labour allocated to provision,

meaning the production of food, the operation and repair of infrastructure, and the care

required to sustain the population, and let λ be the number of persons whose needs are

met per unit of provisioning labour, in the same units. Provision for the whole population

requires λLs ≥N, so that Ls ≥N/λ. The labour remaining for everything outside the

provisioning sector is therefore at most

         L −N ,     or as a fraction of the labour supply,    1 −N               λ                                         λL,

which equals 1 −1/λ under the normalization L = N, that is, one unit of labour per person,

and is smaller when L < N, as when some persons are dependents. The expressions assume

L > 0 and are meaningful only if λL ≥N.  If λL < N they are negative and denote a

provisioning shortfall and not an available residual. Because the accounting is in units of

labour, mixed roles and part-time work are accommodated. The residual measures the

capacity to support activities outside provisioning in general: education, research, art, play,

governance, and care not counted as provision, together with any activity whose rewards have

become detached from its purposes. It must not be read as a quantity of wireheading, since

most of what it supports may be valuable. The limit says only that the capacity to support

activity beyond provisioning is ﬁnite and depends on the productivity of provisioning labour.

That productivity, λ, is not ﬁxed. It varies with technology, and advances in automation

may raise it, which is one reason the design of machines that perform and display ordinary

maintenance bears on the question.

   The ﬁrst requirement of viability concerns the capacity to detect drift between signal

and purpose. This capacity cannot be derived from material accounting. It requires that

some participants are placed to notice divergence, that they are independent of the reward


                                       16

structure being assessed, that they have access to the relevant information, and that they

have the authority or connections through which their observations bear on decisions. These

properties are not captured by a numerical proportion of the population, since a few well-

placed participants may suﬃce where many without standing do not. The requirement is

therefore qualitative, a matter of authority, independence, access and connection, and the

analysis supplies no proportion for it. Its failure can occur in a society that is materially

capable of supporting a great deal of display-oriented activity and that is nevertheless unable

to correct itself.

   The ﬁlm Minority Report, loosely based on a 1956 short story by Philip K. Dick, oﬀers a

suggestive image of this requirement [8, 33]. As the premise is usually summarized, specially

gifted persons, the precogs, produce visions of future crimes on which an institution acts,

and because there are several of them their visions can diﬀer. The record of a dissenting

vision is the minority report of the title. In the ﬁlm, such diﬀering visions are purged from

the records, which preserves an appearance of infallibility [33]. An institution that acts on

such outputs has reason to present them as unanimous, since its authority rests on appearing

reliable.

   The image can be read as an analogy for any arrangement in which a small class of

specialists produces predictions or estimates on which an organization acts. Quantitative

analysts who model risk, and programmers who build the systems that classify and score,

may be thought of as occupying such positions in relation to the businesses and institutions

that employ them. The analogy captures a position and not a person. Unlike the precogs,

analysts are paid, can leave, and can dissent in public, and the comparison should not be

taken to suggest otherwise. What it indicates is a recurring structure. The organization

consumes a signal from a few producers, the credibility of the signal rests on its appearing

singular and conﬁdent, and the alternative models, the stated uncertainties and the dissenting

estimates, which are the minority reports of the arrangement, are the ﬁrst things to be

discarded when they complicate a decision. Curtis argues in the interview discussed above

that the concept of risk came to organize managerial and ﬁnancial life from the 1990s onward,

and that this orientation tends toward the preservation of stability [4]. If that interpretation

is accepted, the pressure to present risk estimates as settled is a particular case of the

pressure to reproduce a stable form described in the preceding section.

   The premise also illustrates the diﬀerence between redundancy and independence. Several

sources provide protection only if their failure mechanisms diﬀer. Sources that share a failure

mechanism fail together, and the appearance of several concordant judgments can mislead.

Nor does the preservation of a dissent establish that the dissent is correct. The defensible

principle is that potentially relevant disagreement must remain available for evaluation,

together with procedures for assessing its signiﬁcance. A dissenting record that exists but is



                                       17

not permitted to inform decisions, or that is treated automatically as malfunction, fails the

conditions of informed assessment and route to intervention stated in this essay. A dissenting

record that is accepted automatically fails diﬀerently, since it substitutes one unexamined

authority for another.

   The second requirement of viability concerns the diversity of modes of work. Societies

depend heavily on roles that formalize, model and optimize, such as programming, statistics

and economic analysis, and they have good reason to value those roles and to extend authority

to those who perform them.  It is plausible that part of the deference such roles attract

derives from this dependence, since the society knows that its systems of provision, ﬁnance

and communication cannot run without them. Deference of this kind is not unreasonable,

but it carries two risks. The ﬁrst is that formalization handles only what can be made legible,

in the sense developed in Scott’s account [29]. The care, tacit skill and local repair that

formal systems presuppose are performed by others and go unrecorded, so that a society

composed predominantly of formalizing roles would lack the people who supply what the

formal layer omits. The second is that a population engaged in similar modes of work shares

error modes. The blind spots of the formal layer would then be common to nearly everyone

placed to notice them, which weakens the capacity for correction. A diversity of working

methods can reduce such shared blind spots, although it does not establish a maximum

permissible share of formalizing roles. Deference also bears on the minority report, since the

standing granted to a dependable source of estimates makes a dissenting estimate harder to

hear.

  An earlier essay by the present author argues in a parallel way about exploratory cognition.

A society in which every citizen behaved as a researcher would deplete its reserves of order,

so such cognition must remain selective, a minority trait supported by institutional structure

and by the maintenance and care of others, within a spectrum of cognitive roles whose

diversity contributes to resilience [11]. The same structure applies here, with an important

qualiﬁcation. The requirement concerns roles and modes of work and not kinds of people.

The same person may formalize in one setting and care or repair in another, and nothing in

the argument implies that those who formalize are lesser or unusual. The requirement yields

no proportion. It says that a society’s allocation across modes of work is itself a variable

to be kept within a viable range, and that high regard for the most formalizable roles can

obscure how much depends on the others.


10. Pleasure, Leisure, and the Objection from Paternalism


The strongest objection to the argument is that it licenses paternalism. Who decides which

satisfactions are legitimate? People may reasonably prefer entertainment, companionship or




                                       18

immersion to activities that an outside observer considers more substantial, and they are

entitled to do so. An argument against wireheading that became an argument that everyone

must remain productive would be both unattractive and self-undermining, since it would

reproduce at the level of a moral theory the very instrumentalism it set out to criticize.

Leisure is not the opposite of a good life, and much that is most worth having consists of

activities pursued for their own sake.

   The response is to locate the concern elsewhere than in the content of anyone’s preferences.

The relevant considerations are agency, dependency and displacement. Can people reconsider

their participation in a given arrangement, and do they have access to the information and

alternatives that reconsideration requires? Do they retain meaningful alternatives, or have

the alternatives been eroded by the growth of the arrangement itself? Are the conditions of

future choice being preserved? And is the arrangement supported by costs that participants

cannot see, or that others must bear? These questions permit criticism without treating

pleasure as suspect. They take a form familiar from capability approaches in political

philosophy, which assess arrangements by the real freedoms they leave people to choose and

to revise their choices, and not by the particular choices people make [30].

   Nozick’s experience machine is instructive in this respect. The standard reading holds

that people decline to plug in because they value contact with reality. A more modest

reading, adequate for the present purposes, is that people value the retention of the capacity

to leave and to be corrected by what lies outside the experience. An arrangement that

provides pleasant experience while preserving that capacity diﬀers importantly from one

that forecloses it. On this view, a person who spends an evening absorbed in a ﬁlm is

not wireheaded, and neither is a community that enjoys shared entertainment. A system

becomes a candidate for the diagnosis when its design makes reconsideration diﬃcult, when

it depends on concealed costs, or when it erodes the material and social conditions under

which alternatives could be pursued.


11. A Universalizability Test for Attention Strategies


The argument of the preceding sections can be given a deontological formulation. The

question is whether the principles organizing an activity could be endorsed as general terms

of cooperation. Kant’s formula of universal law asks whether the maxim of an action could

be willed as a universal law without contradiction or without frustrating the agent’s own

ends [18], and Rawlsian contractualism asks whether principles could be justiﬁed to all those

aﬀected under conditions of fair reasoning [23]. Applied to attention strategies, the test

discriminates between two maxims. “Communicate what you can contribute” can be adopted

by everyone without defeating itself, because its success for one person does not depend




                                       19

on others failing to follow it. “Continually capture more attention than your competitors”

is diﬀerent in kind. Everyone can follow it, and some will continue to win, so it is not

self-defeating in the way that a contradiction would be. What cannot be universalized is

everyone’s achieving superior relative standing, since not everyone can rank above others.

The stronger criticism concerns two further features: the collective costs of escalation,

which rise as each participant matches the eﬀorts of the others, and the presentation of

positional success as a general solution, which misleads those who cannot all achieve it.

These considerations support the ethical argument without making competitive conduct as

such a contradiction under universalization.

   The universalization argument must be qualiﬁed with care. A society requires diﬀerenti-

ated roles, and an occupation need not be suitable for everyone in order to be legitimate.

Not everyone can be a surgeon, a farmer or a conductor, and the fact that a role cannot be

universalized is not an objection to it. The distinction that matters is between a role whose

existence is compatible with a fair general arrangement, and a position whose attractiveness

depends on concealing its reliance on others. The relevant question is whether the governing

arrangement can sustain the diﬀerent roles fairly, with the less visible work recognized

and supported, rather than presenting a position dependent on others’ hidden labour as

everyone’s route to freedom.

   Put diﬀerently, the test applies to the form of the advice and not to the occupation.

An adviser who says that some people can make a living through public communication,

and describes honestly what that depends upon, oﬀers something that can be universalized

as information. An adviser who says that any individual can try, and who treats this as

showing that everyone can succeed simultaneously, oﬀers something that works only so long

as most listeners do not act on it fully. The latter is not thereby shown to be insincere. It is

shown to be a prescription that cannot serve as a general term of cooperation.


12. Preserving the Possibility of Correction


The positive proposal that emerges from the analysis is that rewards should be kept

answerable to their purposes. This is a modest-sounding aim with demanding implications.

Institutions need ways to discover when their preferred measurements cease to track useful

outcomes, and people need room to pursue work whose value appears slowly or resists

continuous publicity. The aim is not to ﬁnd a better metric that will ﬁnally measure

everything correctly. The analysis does not show that every targeted metric must eventually

drift, only that optimization can undermine a proxy under identiﬁable conditions, so that

no metric should be assumed immune. It is to preserve the capacity of a system to detect

and respond to such drift.




                                       20

Several design questions follow, and each involves trade-oﬀs that should be stated

frankly. The ﬁrst concerns protected time for learning and maintenance. Arrangements

that insulate a portion of eﬀort from continuous measurement allow work to proceed whose

value is not yet legible, but they also create room for idleness and for the persistence of

unproductive projects, and distinguishing the two is itself a judgment that metrics cannot

make. The second concerns support for long research horizons. Funding structures with

long commitments allow investigators to pursue questions that do not yield a steady stream

of outputs, at the cost of reduced short-term accountability and the risk of entrenchment.

The third concerns opportunities to leave engagement systems. Exit, in Hirschman’s sense,

supplies a signal about quality that the system cannot easily manufacture [17], but making

exit easy may reduce the revenue of the systems that oﬀer it, and the incentive to resist is

therefore structural. The fourth concerns forms of recognition that do not require permanent

self-advertisement. Mechanisms of peer recognition, apprenticeship lineages, and records

of maintained work can supply acknowledgement of contributions without demanding a

continuous public presence, but they depend on communities with enough stability and

enough shared standards to administer them.

  An additional resource lies in the practice of making the supporting work visible in a form

that is not performance. The didactic design discussed earlier is one instance: a system that

displays its own preparation and repair makes available to observers some of what it takes to

sustain the performance and where it fails. Documentation of ordinary maintenance, public

repair records, and open accounts of failed attempts serve a similar function in institutions.

They are valuable not because they attract attention but because they keep the diﬀerence

between the signal and the activity open to inspection. Russell’s suggestion that the stories

of maintainers be told points to a related use of publicity, which can help people recognize

neglected contributions and secure support for them [28]. Visibility becomes a problem only

when the demands of presentation displace the work, or when recognition never translates

into better conditions for those who do it.

   Observation alone does not amount to correction.  Visibility must support informed

assessment, and informed assessment must have an eﬀective route to intervention. Three

conditions can accordingly be distinguished.  Failure must be observable, so that the

discrepancy can be seen. Observers must be able to make an informed assessment, which

requires that they can understand what they see and diagnose its cause. And informed

assessment must have an eﬀective route to intervention, so that contrary evidence can

alter what the system does. The third condition is the most demanding, since it requires

that people can formulate alternatives, coordinate their eﬀorts, and alter the arrangements

they recognize as defective. Widespread acknowledgement of a defect without any of these

capacities leaves the defect in place. A robot can display its repair process without observers



                                       21

being able to diagnose or alter it, and an institution can publish its failures while ignoring

them. Each measure discussed above can be assessed against all three conditions, and a

measure that secures only the ﬁrst may serve chieﬂy as a further favourable indicator. These

conditions enable correction. They do not guarantee that every proposed correction will be

sound, since a route to intervention can carry mistaken proposals as readily as sound ones,

which is a further reason why the assessment condition matters.

  A ﬁfth question follows from the discussion of hypernormalization, and concerns the

conversion of private knowledge into public information. Where participants understand that

a measure has drifted but face a cost for saying so, the relevant design problem is to lower

that cost or to route the information around it. Anonymous reporting, protected dissent

in review processes, independent audit with real standing, and the routine publication

of negative results are examples of arrangements with this aim, and each has familiar

weaknesses: anonymity can shelter bad faith, protection can be hollow in practice, and audit

can itself become a performed ritual of the kind it was meant to detect. The test of such an

arrangement is whether it changes what participants would be willing to say in public, and

not whether it produces a further favourable indicator.

   None of these measures is oﬀered as a solution. Each can itself be gamed, and each

introduces costs. The claim is the more limited one that a system which has no such measures

is more exposed to the failure described, since nothing within it can register that a failure

has occurred.


13. A World Worth Attending To


The argument may be summarized by returning to the diﬀerence between securing attention

and sustaining its objects. A functioning society needs experiences that people enjoy, and

it needs institutions that recognize achievement and communicate it.  It also needs the

material, ecological, intellectual and interpersonal conditions under which enjoyment and

recognition remain possible. These conditions are produced largely by activities that attract

little notice while they succeed. A culture that rewards the capture of attention more

reliably than it rewards the maintenance of what attention is directed toward is likely to

underinvest in precisely those conditions, and its members may be the last to notice, because

the reinforcement they receive will remain strong.

   The deepest danger of wireheading, understood in this extended sense, is not that people

take pleasure in what they do. It is the progressive loss of the capacity to notice and repair

the diﬀerence between feeling rewarded and living well. When that capacity is intact, a

society can enjoy its entertainments, pursue its ambitions and communicate freely, and

correct its course when its satisfactions begin to diverge from its needs. When it is lost, the




                                       22

divergence widens without producing any internal alarm. A common world must therefore

remain available to correct our satisfactions, even when that correction is inconvenient,

unproﬁtable or initially unrewarding. The condition for its remaining available is that some

of what people attend to, and some of what they do, continues to be answerable to something

other than the signal it produces. The principle can be stated in three parts: failure must be

observable, observable failure must be open to informed assessment, and informed assessment

must have an eﬀective route to intervention, which presupposes that alternatives can be

formulated and collective action coordinated. A common world remains corrective only when

encountering contrary evidence can actually alter what the system does. These conditions

enable correction and do not guarantee that each proposed correction is sound.
